a: CAP: in a partition, a distributed system must choose consistency or availability.
Eventual consistency means replicas converge to the same value given enough time without writes.
Strong consistency means reads see the latest committed write.
Sharding splits data across machines by a shard key to scale storage and throughput.
Replication copies data to multiple nodes for durability and read scale.
Leader-follower replication: one primary takes writes; followers replicate.
Queues decouple producers/consumers, buffer spikes, and enable async processing.
CDNs cache static and some dynamic content near users to cut latency.
Rate limiters use counters/tokens (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket) per key.
URL shorteners map short codes to long URLs with a datastore and optional analytics.
Chat systems need presence, fan-out, storage, delivery receipts, and often WebSockets.
Search uses inverted indexes, ranking, sharding, and sometimes ranking ML.
News feeds use push/pull fan-out, ranking, and caching for home timelines.
Design write APIs to be safely retryable using idempotency keys.
Back-of-envelope estimates use orders of magnitude for QPS, storage, and bandwidth.
